transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Oliver Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Wu (CTO - Argent), Priya Rao (ML Eng - Argent), Laura Kim (Head of Security - Argent)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick discovery focused on model selection for a multi-lingual customer-facing product. Key constraints: long context (documents + chat), support for tool/function-calling, mix of hosted vs private (data residency) options, and need for SOC2 artifacts. Discussed open model candidates and performance/latency/cost tradeoffs. Agreed to share benchmarks and pricing, and to schedule POC kickoff once prompts and volume estimates provided.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual support, tool-calling, hosting modes (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), security/compliance, POC scope

Transcript:
00:00 Oliver Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we have Oliver and Maya from Redwood, and i think Daniel, Priya and Laura are on from Argent?
00:07 Daniel Wu: yep that's right, thanks for setting this up. we are evaluating options for model selection, sort of high level — want to understand which open models make sense for our use case and whether we should go Hosted, Dedicated or Private.
00:22 Maya Patel: awesome. quick question on scope: is this primarily customer support chat with long docs attached, or more generative assistant for workflows?
00:29 Priya Rao: mostly customer support chat + a knowledge base, but we also have a small workflow automation component that needs tool-calling (calendar, ticket create). also multi-lingual — english + spanish + simplified chinese initially.
00:41 Laura Kim: and, from a security perspective, some conversations will contain PII. we need to understand data residency and KMS options.
00:50 Oliver Chen: great, that gives us good context. so three main axes: model capability (multilingual + tool-calling), context length (you mentioned docs, how long are we talking?), and hosting/security requirements.
01:05 Priya Rao: typical thread could be 2–3 long docs, each around 10–20k characters; worst-case we may want to pin 50–60k tokens for context including KB snippets. not sure exact tokens conversion but big.
01:20 Maya Patel: ok so long context is definitely in the 32k to 128k neighborhood depending on how you count. for open models we typically compare Llama2-style families, Mistral, and newer long-context variants. with Redwood you can pick models that we've validated for latency and memory patterns but if you need 50–60k tokens we usually recommend models that have explicit long-context support or chunk + retrieval patterns.
01:42 Daniel Wu: what about tool-calling? we've seen function calling from a couple of vendors, is that something Redwood supports across models or only specific ones?
01:51 Maya Patel: we support structured tool-calling at the API layer — you can register tools and call them via a function schema. on the runtime side, some models are better at following structured schemas out of the box; others need a thin instruction layer. we also have function/tool calling examples for our hosted endpoints and for Dedicated/Private deployments.
02:08 Laura Kim: and for Private, do you integrate with our KMS? we need HSM-backed keys for encryption at rest.
02:15 Oliver Chen: yes, Private deployments can be configured to use customer-managed KMS/HSM. Dedicated also supports customer KMS in many setups, Hosted has envelope encryption with customer key options for enterprise. we'll share the exact matrix in the security pack.
02:28 Priya Rao: latency is a concern — our peak concurrent chat sessions may be 150–200 with spikes. cost is also a big factor; we can't run a huge model for every request.
02:39 Maya Patel: that's the classic latency vs cost tradeoff. some customers use a small fast model for classification/routing and only escalate to a larger long-context model when needed. Redwood runtime supports smart routing and automatic fallback to cheaper variants to keep cost down. we can show you per-route dashboards so you can see token and latency breakdowns.
02:58 Daniel Wu: curious about quantized models — do you validate the quality impact when using 4-bit quantization for these open models?
03:04 Maya Patel: yes, we include quantization profiles in Redwood Optimize recommendations. we run benchmarks on a few datasets to estimate quality delta and cost impact. for some models the delta is negligible, for others you may need 8-bit for high f1 on complex tasks.
03:21 Priya Rao: what open models do customers commonly pick for multi-lingual and long context?
03:26 Maya Patel: recently we've seen folks try Llama 2-70B variants, Mistral long context forks, and some newer community models specialized for long sequences. There's also a pattern: use an embedding+retrieval pipeline for very large KBs to avoid pinning massive contexts, and then use a long-context model for session state or documents that truly need it.
03:44 Daniel Wu: if we go with retrieval, how does Redwood handle caching and latency for embeddings lookups?
03:49 Maya Patel: we do automatic prefix/KV caching and workload-aware batching; embeddings retrieval is usually done in a vector DB you control and our runtime can integrate, but we can also host vector indexes. caching helps a lot — repeated KB lookups have much lower latency.
04:05 Laura Kim: on compliance, SOC2 is must-have. do you have an artifact bundle we can review?
04:10 Oliver Chen: yes we'll send the security pack with SOC2 attestation, ISO notes, and an RH-Private SOC2 row if needed. I'll include a single-sheet mapping showing which artifacts apply to Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
04:22 Priya Rao: for multilingual, are there open models that perform well on simplified chinese? we've found some models degrade outside of english.
04:30 Maya Patel: correct, english is often best. Mistral variants with multilingual tuning, Llama-large tuned forks, and community models targeted at asian languages are options. we recommend you run your own evals with a target test set — we'll provide an eval harness and a multilingual benchmark template.
04:48 Daniel Wu: ok sounds good. what's the expected turnaround for a POC?
04:52 Oliver Chen: once we have sample prompts, a small test set, and your volume estimate, SE team can configure a 30-day pilot — usually spinning up Dedicated or Hosted sandbox in a week, Private depends on networking (VPC/on-prem) and can take 2–4 weeks.
05:05 Priya Rao: we probably want a Dedicated pilot to test throughput and noise isolation, but if Private is required for production we need to validate that path early.
05:13 Maya Patel: that's reasonable — Dedicated is a good step for predictable throughput without the full Private ops overhead. for Private we can run a small on-prem package for air-gapped proof if needed.
05:23 Daniel Wu: can you run benchmarks with our prompts? we want to see latency p50/p95 and cost estimates.
05:28 Maya Patel: yes — we'll ask you to upload sample prompts and a few representative KB documents. we'll run throughput and latency benchmarks across candidate models and quantization levels and return a results sheet.
05:38 Laura Kim: noted. on audit logging — we require immutable logs and retention controls.
05:43 Oliver Chen: Redwood Console provides per-token traces and retention policies. on Private you control retention entirely; Dedicated gives you extended retention options as an add-on. we'll detail this in the security pack.
05:56 (pause, background keyboard noise)
06:10 Daniel Wu: another question — tool calling reliability. if the model mis-invokes a tool, do you have a middleware layer to validate outputs before execution?
06:18 Maya Patel: yes that's a best practice. our SDK includes a validator pattern and we recommend a middleware step to canonicalize outputs and check schemas before executing actions. building an allowlist and assertion layer is common.
06:31 Priya Rao: ok, let's talk concrete models. we have to balance token budget: we'd like to keep per-interaction token cost under X (they left X unspecified but later gave estimate) — like maybe target <$0.02 per session?
06:44 Oliver Chen: cost per session depends on model size, quantization, and how much of the KB you include in context. using retrieval plus a smaller session model usually keeps costs controlled. we'll run a cost projection in the pricing doc.
06:55 Daniel Wu: are there any Redwood-verified performance profiles?
06:59 Maya Patel: we publish a model catalog with validated perf numbers (latency, mem footprint, token cost) across common instance types. it's not exhaustive but it's a good starting point. we'll attach the catalog link and a short spreadsheet showing p50/p95 numbers for candidate models.
07:16 Priya Rao: one more latency question — for long-context inference, do you stream partial results or buffer until completion?
07:23 Maya Patel: we support streaming responses on compatible models and SDKs. streaming reduces perceived latency for users. note that some long-context kernels do chunked computation so streaming behavior can vary, we'll clarify per-model.
07:36 Daniel Wu: does Redwood do automatic kernel selection? we run on NVIDIA A100s and some customers are on newer H100-based infra.
07:43 Maya Patel: runtime chooses kernels based on architecture and hardware. for Dedicated we can provision specific instance types and tune kernels; for Private we can run on whatever infra you provide and we will surface tuning recommendations.
07:55 Oliver Chen: to recap, so far: Argent needs multilingual + tool-calling + long context, prefer Dedicated pilot, security needs SOC2 + KMS/HSM + audit logs. next steps: we will send pricing and security docs; Maya will share a benchmark template; Argent will provide sample prompts and volume estimates.
08:18 Daniel Wu: yes that matches. one quick nit — we're considering fallbacks to a smaller on-device style model for offline mode, is that possible?
08:24 Maya Patel: Private gives you the most flexibility — you can run smaller on-prem models for offline mode and use Redwood routing to decide online vs offline.
08:33 (short cross-talk)
08:45 Priya Rao: any gotchas around tokenization differences across models, especially for chinese?
08:51 Maya Patel: absolutely. tokenization changes can dramatically affect token counts. our benchmark template accounts for tokenizer normalization and we'll compute tokenized lengths for each model we test.
09:06 Daniel Wu: ok when can we expect the docs?
09:09 Oliver Chen: i'll send the pricing/comparison + security pack by friday (2027-09-17). maya will send the benchmark template tomorrow (2027-09-16).
09:18 Laura Kim: great, i'll put together a short list of SOC2 questions and controls we need clarification on.
09:23 Priya Rao: i'll work on getting you a 200-300 prompt test set including english, spanish, and simplified chinese examples.
09:30 Oliver Chen: perfect — once we have those we'll schedule the SE-led POC kickoff.
09:35 (background: someone muting/unmuting)
09:45 Daniel Wu: on competitors, we've also looked at OpenAI's function calling and Anthropic for safety guardrails. any major differences we should call out?
09:53 Maya Patel: open vendors vary on function-calling ergonomics and model openness; Redwood is model-agnostic so you can choose open models and manage them across Hosted/Dedicated/Private. safety tooling is part of our offering, but if you need specialized guardrails we can plug in policy layers.
10:10 Oliver Chen: cool. anything else from Argent?
10:13 Laura Kim: one last ask — can you include network diagrams for Dedicated vs Private in the security pack? that helps our infra team.
10:19 Oliver Chen: yes we'll include sample VPC diagrams and an on-prem network checklist.
10:24 Priya Rao: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
10:28 (end of captured transcript)
